content: CD36, also referred to as platelet glycoprotein 4, fatty acid translocase (FAT), scavenger receptor class B member 3 (SCARB3), glycoprotein 88 (GP88), glycoprotein IIIb (GPIIIB), or glycoprotein IV (GPIV), is a transmembrane protein encoded by the CD36 gene in humans. This protein is expressed on the surface of various cell types in vertebrates and is involved in the uptake of fatty acids into cells. CD36 belongs to the class B scavenger receptor family and interacts with a wide range of ligands, including collagen, thrombospondin, oxidized low-density lipoprotein (oxLDL), native lipoproteins, oxidized phospholipids, long-chain fatty acids, and erythrocytes infected with Plasmodium falciparum. Studies in genetically modified rodents suggest that CD36 plays a role in fatty acid metabolism, cardiovascular diseases, taste perception, and the processing of dietary fats in the intestine. It has also been implicated in conditions such as glucose intolerance, atherosclerosis, hypertension, diabetes, cardiomyopathy, and Alzheimer’s disease. Structure of CD36 Primary Structure In humans, rats, and mice, CD36 is composed of 472 amino acids, with a predicted molecular weight of approximately 53 kDa. However, due to extensive glycosylation, its apparent molecular weight is approximately 88 kDa, as determined by SDS-PAGE. Tertiary Structure The amino acid sequence of CD36, analyzed using Kyte-Doolittle hydrophobicity plots, suggests the presence of hydrophobic regions at both the Nand C-termini, which are sufficient to span the cellular membrane. This structural arrangement gives CD36 a hairpin-like topology, with α-helices at the termini traversing the membrane and a large extracellular loop. This topology is supported by transfection experiments using deletion mutants. Based on the crystal structure of the homologous SCARB2 protein, CD36 is predicted to have an extracellular domain with an antiparallel β-barrel core surrounded by short α-helices. A hydrophobic transport tunnel is also proposed to exist within the structure. Disulfide bonds between four of the six cysteine residues in the extracellular loop are essential for proper intracellular processing and transport of CD36 to the plasma membrane, although their role in the mature protein's function remains unclear. Posttranslational Modifications CD36 undergoes several posttranslational modifications, including glycosylation and palmitoylation. It is modified with four palmitoyl chains, two on each intracellular domain, which likely facilitate its association with the membrane and lipid rafts, structures that are critical for some CD36 functions. Additionally, CD36 can be phosphorylated at specific residues (Y62, T92, T323), ubiquitinated (K56, K469, K472), and acetylated (K52, K56, K166, K231, K394, K398, K403). The functional significance of these modifications is still under investigation. Protein-Protein Interactions In its unbound state, CD36 exists primarily as a monomer on the cell membrane. However, upon binding to thrombospondin, CD36 undergoes dimerization, which is thought to be critical for its role in signal transduction. Genetics of CD36 The CD36 gene is located on chromosome 7q11.2 in humans and spans over 32 kilobases, comprising 15 exons. Both the 5' and 3' untranslated regions (UTRs) contain introns. Exons 1, 2, and part of exon 3, as well as exon 15, are non-coding. The N-terminal cytoplasmic and transmembrane domains are encoded by exon 3, while the C-terminal domains are encoded by exon 14. The extracellular domain is encoded by the central 11 exons. Alternative splicing of the UTRs results in at least two mRNA isoforms. The transcription of CD36 is regulated by the PPAR/RXR nuclear receptor heterodimer, and its expression can be upregulated by ligands such as thiazolidinediones (anti-diabetic drugs) and 9-cis-retinoic acid (a vitamin A metabolite). Tissue Distribution CD36 is expressed on various cell types, including platelets, erythrocytes, monocytes, differentiated adipocytes, skeletal muscle cells, mammary epithelial cells, spleen cells, and certain skin microdermal endothelial cells. Functions of CD36 CD36 is a member of the class B scavenger receptor family, which includes receptors involved in selective cholesteryl ester uptake, such as SR-BI and LIMP-II. CD36 interacts with numerous ligands, including collagen types I and IV, thrombospondin, oxidized LDL, long-chain fatty acids, and Plasmodium falciparum-infected erythrocytes. On macrophages, CD36 forms part of a non-opsonic receptor complex (CD36/αVβ3) involved in phagocytosis. CD36 has been implicated in hemostasis, thrombosis, malaria, inflammation, lipid metabolism, and atherogenesis. Upon ligand binding, CD36 and its ligand are internalized via an actin-dependent mechanism involving Src-family kinases, JNK, and Rho-family GTPases. This process is independent of macropinocytosis and is not affected by inhibitors of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase or Na+/H+ exchange. CD36 ligands can also induce sterile inflammation by promoting the assembly of a Toll-like receptor 4/6 heterodimer. Additionally, CD36 has been linked to store-operated calcium flux, phospholipase A2 activation, and prostaglandin E2 production. The uptake and signaling of long-chain fatty acids by CD36 can be irreversibly inhibited by sulfo-N-succinimidyl oleate (SSO), which binds to lysine 164 within a hydrophobic pocket shared by several CD36 ligands. Clinical Significance Malaria CD36 serves as a major sequestration receptor for Plasmodium falciparum-infected erythrocytes on microvascular endothelial cells. The parasite's erythrocyte membrane protein 1 (PfEMP1) binds to CD36, facilitating cytoadherence. Mutations in the CD36 gene, particularly in exon 5, have been associated with reduced risk of severe malaria, suggesting a protective role. However, CD36 is not the sole determinant of malaria severity. In mouse models, CD36 has been shown to mediate immune responses to malaria, including cytokine induction and parasite clearance. CD36 Deficiency and Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia CD36 deficiency, also known as the Naka-negative phenotype, is more common in certain populations, such as Africans and Asians, and can lead to refractoriness to platelet transfusion. CD36 deficiency is classified into type 1 (absence on platelets and monocytes) and type 2 (absence on platelets only). Mutations in the CD36 gene, such as T1264G and C478T, have been identified in individuals with this condition. Fatty Acid Uptake CD36 is associated with myocardial fatty acid uptake, and its dysfunction has been linked to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Tuberculosis A member of the CD36 family has been shown to be essential for the phagocytosis of Mycobacterium tuberculosis into macrophage phagosomes. Obesity CD36 is involved in the ability to taste fats, and its expression in taste bud cells is reduced in obese animals. This reduction may impair lipid taste sensitivity and contribute to altered dietary behaviors in obesity. In humans, CD36 expression levels correlate with oral fat sensitivity, suggesting a potential role in obesity-related therapies. Cellular Senescence CD36 upregulation during senescence contributes to membrane remodeling and the production of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, a phenomenon known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). Cancer CD36 regulates angiogenesis and may promote cancer cell migration and proliferation in certain cancers, such as hepatocellular carcinoma and glioblastoma. Targeting CD36-mediated fatty acid uptake may represent a therapeutic strategy for cancer treatment. Related Proteins CD36 is related to other human scavenger receptors, including SCARB1 and SCARB2.
